disease_symptoms.s1: Circular black spots with fringed, feathery margins appear on the upper surface of leaves.
disease_symptoms.s2: Leaf tissue surrounding the dark spots turns bright yellow (chlorosis).
disease_symptoms.s3: Severe premature leaf drop (defoliation) beginning from lower branches upward, weakening the bush.
disease_symptoms.s4: Raised purplish-red to black blistering lesions may develop on young canes and flower buds.

disease_causes.c1: Fungal spores overwinter in fallen dead leaves and infected cane lesions.
disease_causes.c2: Prolonged leaf wetness (at least 7 hours) with temperatures between 68°F and 75°F (20°C - 24°C).
disease_causes.c3: Overhead watering, rainfall splashing, and high relative humidity above 85%.
disease_causes.c4: Dense canopy growth with poor air circulation trapping moisture around the foliage.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant disease-resistant rose cultivars (e.g., Knock Out, Rugosa, or modern floribundas).
disease_prevention.p2: Water at the base of the bush early in the morning using drip or soaker hose; avoid wetting foliage.
disease_prevention.p3: Space bushes 3 to 4 feet apart and prune interior crossing branches to promote rapid drying airflow.
disease_prevention.p4: Rake and burn/dispose of all fallen autumn leaves; never compost black-spot infected rose debris.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced Rose Fertilizer (NPK 10-15-10 or 12-6-12) enriched with Magnesium and Iron.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Apply Potassium (K) (Sulfate of Potash) in spring to fortify epidermal cell walls against fungal hyphae.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Avoid high-nitrogen synthetic fertilizers mid-season, as soft lush vegetative growth is highly susceptible.
fertilizer_recommendation.f4: Top-dress with 2 inches of aged pine bark mulch to prevent soil-borne spore splashing during rain.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Tebuconazole or Myclobutanil (Systemic triazole fungicides applied every 10-14 days during wet periods).
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Chlorothalonil (Broad-spectrum protective contact fungicide, ideal for early spring preventative sprays).
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Copper Hydroxide / Liquid Copper Fungicide (Apply during dormant winter season to kill overwintering spores).
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf4: Mancozeb or Captan (Effective preventative protectant sprays applied before rain events).

organic_remedies.org1: Cold-pressed Neem Oil Spray (0.5% - 1% concentration with mild organic soap) applied every 7 days.
organic_remedies.org2: Potassium Bicarbonate / Baking Soda Solution (1 tbsp baking soda + 1 tsp horticultural oil per gallon of water).
organic_remedies.org3: Bacillus amyloliquefaciens / Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide sprays to outcompete fungal spores.
organic_remedies.org4: Liquid Kelp & Seaweed Foliar Spray to stimulate plant systemic acquired resistance (SAR).

disease_control.ctrl1: Immediately hand-pick and dispose of all spotted leaves to curb spore dispersal.
disease_control.ctrl2: Prune infected canes 2 inches below visible discoloration and sterilize shears with 70% alcohol.
disease_control.ctrl3: Apply an approved preventative fungicide spray at the first sign of new spring leaf emergence.

disease_symptoms.s1: White to grayish-white powdery talcum-like fungal patches on young leaves, shoots, and unopened buds.
disease_symptoms.s2: Infected young leaves become twisted, curled, puckered, and blistered.
disease_symptoms.s3: Flower buds fail to open or produce deformed, stunted blossoms.
disease_symptoms.s4: Severe infection causes foliage to turn reddish-purple or brown and drop prematurely.

disease_causes.c1: Favored by warm dry days (70°F - 80°F) accompanied by cool, high-humidity nights (90-99% RH).
disease_causes.c2: Unlike most fungi, powdery mildew spores germinate in high humidity WITHOUT requiring liquid water on leaves.
disease_causes.c3: Over-fertilization with nitrogen causing excessive soft young succulent growth.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant roses in full sunlight (minimum 6-8 hours daily); sunlight inhibits powdery mildew germination.
disease_prevention.p2: Ensure wide spacing between bushes and prune center branches for maximum breeze circulation.
disease_prevention.p3: Hose down foliage with water in the bright mid-morning; free water actually washes off and lyses mildew spores!

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Switch to low-nitrogen, high-potassium & phosphorus blends (e.g. NPK 5-10-15).
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Foliar application of Soluble Silica / Potassium Silicate to strengthen epidermal defenses.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Supplement with Calcium Nitrate early in the season to enhance cellular rigidity.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Myclobutanil (Immunox) or Propiconazole (Systemic curative and preventative fungicide).
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Sulfur-based Dust or Wettable Sulfur Spray (Never apply when temperatures exceed 85°F/29°C).
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Triforine or Trifloxystrobin for commercial and large garden rose collections.

organic_remedies.org1: Milk Spray: 1 part milk to 9 parts water sprayed in direct sunlight (milk proteins create natural antiseptics).
organic_remedies.org2: Horticultural Oil or Jojoba Oil sprays to smother and eradicate existing mycelial mats.
organic_remedies.org3: Potassium Bicarbonate (MilStop) 2 to 3 tablespoons per gallon of water.

disease_control.ctrl1: Prune away severely distorted shoot tips and deformed buds.
disease_control.ctrl2: Thoroughly spray tops and undersides of leaves with organic sulfur or neem oil every 5-7 days.
disease_control.ctrl3: Clean garden tools after working on infected plants to prevent transmission.

disease_symptoms.s1: Bright orange, powdery pustules (uredinia) on the undersides of leaves.
disease_symptoms.s2: Corresponding light yellow or chlorotic flecks on the upper leaf surface.
disease_symptoms.s3: Pustules turn black in late summer/autumn as overwintering teliospores form.
disease_symptoms.s4: Severe defoliation, twig dieback, and general loss of plant vigor.

disease_causes.c1: Cool to moderate temperatures (55°F - 65°F / 13°C - 18°C) and continuous moisture for 2 to 4 hours.
disease_causes.c2: Overwintering in infected dead leaves, leaf mulch, and stem cankers.

disease_prevention.p1: Collect and destroy all fallen leaves before winter.
disease_prevention.p2: Avoid overhead watering; keep leaves dry.
disease_prevention.p3: Annual hard dormant pruning to remove overwintering stem cankers.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced organic rose fertilizer enriched with kelp meal, rock phosphate, and bone meal.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Avoid late-season nitrogen applications that delay winter dormancy.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Mancozeb, Chlorothalonil, or Myclobutanil sprayed at 7-10 day intervals during cool damp weather.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Dormant spray of Lime-Sulfur in late winter before bud-break.

organic_remedies.org1: Sulfur sprays and bio-fungicides containing Bacillus subtilis.
organic_remedies.org2: Neem oil foliar sprays applied early morning.

disease_control.ctrl1: Prune out and bag infected branches; do not drop infected leaves onto garden beds.
disease_control.ctrl2: Begin preventative fungicide applications in early spring when new shoots reach 2-4 inches.

disease_symptoms.s1: Glossy, deep green, uniformly colored foliage with clean serrated margins.
disease_symptoms.s2: Sturdy, erect canes with healthy pith and firm green bark.
disease_symptoms.s3: Well-formed flower buds with clean sepals and vibrant blossom development.
disease_symptoms.s4: Zero spotting, powdery residues, rust pustules, or insect webbing.

disease_causes.c1: Proper cultural care: adequate sunlight, balanced soil nutrition, and optimal irrigation.

disease_prevention.p1: Maintain 6-8 hours of direct sunlight and 3-foot spacing.
disease_prevention.p2: Inspect leaf undersides weekly for early detection of aphids, spider mites, or black spot.
disease_prevention.p3: Sanitize pruners between bushes using rubbing alcohol.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Apply slow-release balanced rose food (NPK 10-10-10 or 8-12-8) every 4-6 weeks during blooming season.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Add 1 cup of alfalfa meal and 1 tbsp of Epsom salt (Magnesium Sulfate) around the drip line in spring.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Cease nitrogen fertilizing 6 weeks before first anticipated frost to harden off canes.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: No chemical pesticides required for healthy roses.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Optional preventative botanical dormant spray (horticultural oil) in late winter.

organic_remedies.org1: Beneficial companion planting with Alliums (garlic/chives) and Marigolds to deter aphids and nematodes.
organic_remedies.org2: Compost tea foliar drench monthly to sustain healthy phyllosphere microflora.

disease_control.ctrl1: Continue regular deadheading of spent blooms to channel energy into vigorous root and shoot systems.

disease_symptoms.s1: Brown to black circular spots developing distinctive concentric rings like a target board.
disease_symptoms.s2: Yellow chlorotic halo surrounding leaf lesions on older bottom leaves first.
disease_symptoms.s3: Progressive upward defoliation exposing green tomato fruit to sunscald.
disease_symptoms.s4: Dark, sunken, leathery lesions at the stem end of fruits.

disease_causes.c1: Pathogen overwinters on solanaceous crop residue and volunteer tomato/potato weeds in soil.
disease_causes.c2: Favored by warm humid weather (75°F - 85°F / 24°C - 29°C) with alternating wet and dry periods.
disease_causes.c3: Soil splash from heavy rains or overhead sprinklers transferring spores to lowest leaves.

disease_prevention.p1: Practice strict 3 to 4-year crop rotation; avoid planting tomatoes after potatoes, peppers, or eggplants.
disease_prevention.p2: Prune all bottom leaves up to 18 inches above the ground once plants reach 3 feet tall.
disease_prevention.p3: Mulch generously with clean straw, black plastic, or wood chips to create a splash barrier.
disease_prevention.p4: Stake or cage plants upright to maintain good airflow and dry foliage.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced Tomato Fertilizer with lower nitrogen and high potassium/calcium (e.g. NPK 5-10-10 or 4-18-38).
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Apply Calcium Nitrate to prevent blossom end rot and strengthen epidermal resistance to Alternaria toxins.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which creates dense, humid canopy foliage.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Chlorothalonil (Daconil) - Highly effective protective contact fungicide applied every 7-10 days.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Copper Hydroxide / Copper Octanoate (Liquid Copper) approved for organic and conventional growers.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Azoxystrobin or Mancozeb - Commercial preventative and early curative fungicides.

organic_remedies.org1: Bacillus subtilis or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens (Serenade ASO) bio-fungicides.
organic_remedies.org2: Copper sulfate / Bordeaux mixture sprayed early in the morning.
organic_remedies.org3: Potassium Bicarbonate spray (3 tbsp per gallon water) to alter leaf surface pH against spores.

disease_control.ctrl1: Strip and bag all infected bottom leaves immediately at first sign of target spots.
disease_control.ctrl2: Do not work in tomato patch when foliage is wet from dew or rain to prevent spreading spores.
disease_control.ctrl3: Apply preventative fungicide immediately after rain events during warm summer periods.

disease_symptoms.s1: Large, irregular, water-soaked, dark olive-green to black greasy lesions on leaves and stems.
disease_symptoms.s2: Delicate white fuzzy fungal-like growth on the undersides of leaves during humid morning conditions.
disease_symptoms.s3: Stems turn dark brown to black and collapse rapidly.
disease_symptoms.s4: Fruits develop large, firm, greasy brown lesions with bumpy texture, ruining the harvest.

disease_causes.c1: Cool, wet, cloudy weather (60°F - 70°F / 15°C - 21°C) with relative humidity above 90%.
disease_causes.c2: Windborne sporangia that can travel several miles on air currents from infected fields.
disease_causes.c3: Infected cull potato piles or volunteer plants serving as seasonal inoculum sources.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant certified disease-free transplants and resistant hybrids (e.g., Defiant, Mountain Magic, Iron Lady).
disease_prevention.p2: Ensure maximum spacing between rows and stake plants for rapid leaf drying.
disease_prevention.p3: Destroy all volunteer tomato and potato seedlings early in spring.
disease_prevention.p4: Never compost late blight infected plants; bag and dispose of in municipal trash or burn.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: NPK 8-15-36 formulation enriched with Potassium and Phosphorus to boost plant immunity.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Apply Phosphite / Potassium Phosphite (0-0-28) foliar sprays to activate systemic plant defense pathways.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Avoid high-nitrogen fertilizers that create soft vegetative tissue vulnerable to zoospore penetration.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Cymoxanil + Mancozeb (Curzate) - Rapid translaminar curative and protectant action.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Mandipropamid (Revus) or Dimethomorph (Forum) - Highly specialized Oomycete fungicides.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Copper Hydroxide applied preventatively before rain storms when late blight warnings are issued.

organic_remedies.org1: Fixed Copper fungicides (Nordox or Badge X2) applied preventatively every 5 days during blight weather.
organic_remedies.org2: Bio-fungicides containing Streptomyces lydicus or Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.
organic_remedies.org3: Hydrogen Dioxide / Peroxyacetic acid (OxiDate) sanitizing spray to kill surface spores.

disease_control.ctrl1: Act immediately upon first symptom: remove infected foliage or entire plant if stem is infected.
disease_control.ctrl2: Notify neighboring gardeners, as Phytophthora spores travel rapidly on wind.
disease_control.ctrl3: Harvest mature green fruits immediately from unaffected vines before blight spreads to fruit.

disease_symptoms.s1: Vibrant deep green foliage with uniform chlorophyll distribution across all leaves.
disease_symptoms.s2: Stems are thick, sturdy, and covered with healthy trichome glandular hairs.
disease_symptoms.s3: Abundant bright yellow blossoms with successful fruit set and smooth skin.
disease_symptoms.s4: Zero spots, chlorosis, curling, greasy lesions, or pest damage.

disease_causes.c1: Optimal environmental balance: 6-8 hours of direct sun, consistent watering, and fertile soil.

disease_prevention.p1: Maintain 2-3 inches of organic straw or wood mulch under plants.
disease_prevention.p2: Prune suckers and lowest leaves touching the ground to prevent soil-borne fungal spores.
disease_prevention.p3: Water deeply at ground level using drip emitters; keep leaves dry.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced Tomato Food (NPK 4-18-38 or 5-10-10) with Calcium, Magnesium, and Sulfur.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Side-dress with bone meal and compost when fruit first sets to provide slow-release Phosphorus.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Maintain soil pH between 6.2 and 6.8 for optimal nutrient uptake.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: No chemical treatments necessary for healthy plants.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Optional preventative biological drench with mycorrhizal fungi at root zone.

organic_remedies.org1: Companion planting with Basil and French Marigolds to naturally repel hornworms and aphids.
organic_remedies.org2: Compost tea foliar spray to maintain robust beneficial microbial colonies.

disease_control.ctrl1: Support heavy vines with sturdy cages or trellising to prevent fruit contact with soil.

disease_symptoms.s1: Small (less than 1/8 inch), water-soaked, dark brown to black circular lesions on leaves.
disease_symptoms.s2: Lesions often have a distinctive yellow halo and appear greasy on leaf undersides.
disease_symptoms.s3: Leaves turn yellow, dry out, and take on a scorched, ragged appearance.
disease_symptoms.s4: Fruits exhibit small, raised, black blister-like spots that become scabby and rough.

disease_causes.c1: Warm temperatures (75°F - 86°F / 24°C - 30°C) combined with high rainfall, overhead watering, and high humidity.
disease_causes.c2: Bacteria enter through natural openings (stomata) and minor wounds caused by wind, sand, or pruning.
disease_causes.c3: Infected seed or infected volunteer tomato plants.

disease_prevention.p1: Always purchase certified disease-free, hot-water-treated tomato seed.
disease_prevention.p2: Avoid working in wet fields or pruning during damp weather.
disease_prevention.p3: Rotate crops with non-solanaceous plants (corn, beans, brassicas) for minimum 2-3 years.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Maintain balanced NPK (e.g. 5-10-10) with adequate Potassium to thicken cell walls.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Foliar Zinc and Manganese to bolster bacterial defense enzymes.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Avoid high ammonium nitrogen which increases succulent leaf vulnerability.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Copper Hydroxide mixed with Mancozeb (Mancozeb enhances copper bioavailability against resistant Xanthomonas).
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Acibenzolar-S-methyl (Actigard) - Plant defense activator that triggers systemic acquired resistance (SAR).
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Bacteriophages (AgriPhage) - Biological virus spray specifically targeting Xanthomonas strains.

organic_remedies.org1: Liquid Copper Octanoate (Copper soap) sprayed every 7 days.

disease_control.ctrl1: Remove and destroy severely affected leaves immediately.
disease_control.ctrl2: Apply copper + mancozeb tank mix preventatively before rain forecast.
disease_control.ctrl3: Disinfect stakes, cages, and pruning tools with 10% bleach solution.

Tomato___Leaf_Mold.severity: Moderate to High (Especially in High Tunnels/Greenhouses)

disease_symptoms.s1: Pale green or yellow spots with indefinite borders on the upper surface of older leaves.
disease_symptoms.s2: Dense, velvety, olive-green to grayish-purple mold growth on the undersides of leaves directly below yellow spots.
disease_symptoms.s3: Leaves curl, wither, turn completely brown and drop prematurely.
disease_symptoms.s4: Rarely affects fruit directly, but defoliation significantly reduces fruit size and yield.

disease_causes.c1: High relative humidity (>85%) and warm temperatures between 70°F and 75°F (21°C - 24°C).
disease_causes.c2: Common in greenhouses, hoop houses, and dense field plantings with inadequate ventilation.

disease_prevention.p1: Increase airflow and ventilation in greenhouses using horizontal airflow fans.
disease_prevention.p2: Space plants generously (minimum 24-30 inches apart in rows) and prune suckers.
disease_prevention.p3: Use drip irrigation; never wet foliage late in the day.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balance nitrogen with high Potassium and Calcium (NPK 4-18-38).
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Apply soluble Potassium Silicate to harden leaf surfaces against conidial penetration.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Chlorothalonil, Mancozeb, or Copper Hydroxide applied as thorough preventative canopy cover.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Difenoconazole or Azoxystrobin (Quadris Top) for high-value commercial plantings.

organic_remedies.org1: Bio-fungicides like Bacillus subtilis (Serenade) and Streptomyces lydicus (Actinovate).
organic_remedies.org3: Potassium bicarbonate spray (MilStop) to suppress sporulation.

disease_control.ctrl1: Strip infected lower leaves and lower greenhouse humidity below 80% with ventilation.
disease_control.ctrl2: Spray both upper and lower leaf surfaces thoroughly, as the fungus primarily resides underneath.

disease_symptoms.s1: Numerous small (1/16 to 1/8 inch), circular spots with gray or tan centers and dark brown borders.
disease_symptoms.s2: Tiny black specks (pycnidia - spore-bearing structures) visible in the center of mature spots under a hand lens.
disease_symptoms.s3: Leaves turn yellow, wither, and fall off, starting at the bottom and progressing rapidly upward.

disease_causes.c1: Warm temperatures (68°F - 77°F / 20°C - 25°C) and extended periods of high humidity and wet foliage.
disease_causes.c2: Fungus survives in plant debris, nightshade weeds, and horse nettle.

disease_prevention.p1: Mulch plants with clean straw or plastic immediately after transplanting to block soil splash.
disease_prevention.p2: Prune lower 12-18 inches of leaves once plants are established.
disease_prevention.p3: Practice 3-year crop rotation away from tomatoes and potatoes.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: High-potash fertilizer (NPK 5-10-15) to sustain plant vigor through defoliation stress.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Foliar seaweed extract to stimulate recovery growth.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Chlorothalonil (Daconil) applied every 7-10 days starting at first bloom.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Mancozeb or Copper Hydroxide as effective protective options.

organic_remedies.org1: Fixed copper sprays (Bordeaux mixture or Copper Octanoate).
organic_remedies.org2: Bacillus subtilis bio-fungicide sprays applied on 5-day intervals.

disease_control.ctrl1: Remove and destroy infected leaves as soon as first spotted; never compost.
disease_control.ctrl2: Clean up and plow under or burn all plant residue after final harvest.

disease_symptoms.s1: Fine white or yellow speckling (stippling) on the upper surface of leaves.
disease_symptoms.s2: Fine silken webbing visible on leaf undersides, growing tips, and flower clusters.
disease_symptoms.s3: Leaves turn bronze, yellow, dry out, and drop; plants look scorched and dusty.
disease_symptoms.s4: Under a 10x lens, tiny pale yellow or greenish mites with two dark spots are seen moving.

disease_causes.c1: Hot, dry, and dusty weather (above 85°F / 29°C) accelerates their life cycle from 20 days to just 5 days!
disease_causes.c2: Drought stress makes tomato plants sweeter and more attractive to spider mites.
disease_causes.c3: Overuse of broad-spectrum synthetic pyrethroids that kill natural predatory insects.

disease_prevention.p1: Keep plants well-watered and avoid drought stress during heat waves.
disease_prevention.p2: Hose down foliage and garden pathways periodically to knock off mites and reduce dust.
disease_prevention.p3: Encourage natural predators like lady beetles, lacewings, and predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis).

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizers, which stimulate explosive mite reproduction.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Apply foliar seaweed and Potassium Silicate to toughen plant cuticle against mite piercing.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Bifenazate (Acramite) or Abamectin (Agri-Mek) - Specialized targeted miticides.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Spiromesifen (Oberon) - Lipid biosynthesis inhibitor affecting mite eggs and nymphs.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Insecticidal Soap (Potassium salts of fatty acids) targeting soft-bodied mites directly.

organic_remedies.org1: Cold-Pressed Neem Oil (1% emulsion) or Rosemary Oil horticultural spray.
organic_remedies.org2: Release biological predatory mites (Phytoseiulus persimilis or Neoseiulus californicus).
organic_remedies.org3: Sulfur sprays (do not apply within 30 days of oil sprays or when temp > 90°F).

disease_control.ctrl1: Prune and bag heavily webbed shoots and remove them from garden immediately.
disease_control.ctrl2: Spray leaf undersides thoroughly with high-pressure insecticidal soap or neem oil twice a week.

disease_symptoms.s1: Brown circular lesions with concentric rings and distinct yellow chlorotic halos.
disease_symptoms.s2: Lesions may crack open in the center giving a shot-hole appearance.
disease_symptoms.s3: Can cause sunken circular lesions on both green and ripe fruit.

disease_causes.c1: Warm, humid tropical and sub-tropical conditions (68°F - 82°F) with prolonged dew periods.
disease_causes.c2: Survival in crop residues, alternate weed hosts, and volunteer plants.

disease_prevention.p1: Provide wide plant spacing and stake tomatoes to maximize air circulation.
disease_prevention.p2: Rotate crops with non-susceptible grasses and legumes.
disease_prevention.p3: Avoid overhead irrigation.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced NPK fertilizer enriched with Calcium and Potassium.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Avoid excess nitrogen.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Copper Hydroxide.

organic_remedies.org1: Copper fungicides and Bacillus amyloliquefaciens.

disease_control.ctrl1: Prune infected lower foliage immediately and treat with protective fungicide.

disease_symptoms.s1: Upward curling and cupping of leaf margins into small cup-like shapes.
disease_symptoms.s2: Pronounced yellowing (chlorosis) along leaf margins and between veins on young leaves.
disease_symptoms.s3: Severe stunting of young shoots, giving the plant a compact bushy or 'bonsai' appearance.
disease_symptoms.s4: Blossoms drop off readily; virtually zero fruit development if infected when young.

disease_causes.c1: Transmitted exclusively by the Sweetpotato Whitefly / Silverleaf Whitefly (Bemisia tabaci).
disease_causes.c2: Virus is NOT seed-borne or mechanically transmitted by touch; strictly vector-spread.
disease_causes.c3: Warm temperatures that promote explosive whitefly population surges.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant TYLCV-resistant tomato hybrids (e.g., Tycoon, Camaro, Chef's Choice, SV8232TD).
disease_prevention.p2: Install insect-proof exclusion netting (50-mesh) in nurseries and high tunnels.
disease_prevention.p3: Use UV-reflective silver or aluminum mulches to repel incoming whiteflies.
disease_prevention.p4: Deploy yellow sticky cards around plants to monitor and trap whitefly adults.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Foliar Zinc, Iron, and Magnesium to alleviate viral chlorosis stress.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Balanced organic kelp meal to maintain root vitality.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Insecticides targeting the whitefly vector: Imidacloprid, Dinotefuran, or Acetamiprid.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Insect growth regulators (Pyriproxyfen or Buprofezin) to break whitefly breeding cycles.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Note: Fungicides have NO effect on viral diseases.

organic_remedies.org1: Insecticidal Soap + Neem Oil sprays every 4 days to smother whitefly nymphs.
organic_remedies.org2: Introduce biological control wasps (Encarsia formosa or Eretmocerus eremicus).

disease_control.ctrl1: Immediately rogued (uproot) and destroy infected plants; put in sealed plastic bag under sun to kill vector.
disease_control.ctrl2: Do not leave infected plants in garden, as they serve as virus reservoirs for whiteflies to infect other plants.

disease_symptoms.s1: Mottled light and dark green mosaic patterns on foliage.
disease_symptoms.s2: Leaves become distorted, puckered, blistered, or narrow and 'shoestring'-like.
disease_symptoms.s3: Stunted overall plant growth with internal browning (brown wall) of fruit flesh.

disease_causes.c1: Extremely stable virus transmitted mechanically via hands, tools, grafting, and smoking tobacco products.
disease_causes.c2: Can survive in dry plant debris and unwashed greenhouse stakes for years.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant resistant cultivars with the 'Tm-2' or 'Tm-2a' resistance gene.
disease_prevention.p2: Wash hands with soap or skim milk before handling plants; never smoke or use tobacco near tomatoes.
disease_prevention.p3: Disinfect tools between plants with 20% nonfat dry milk solution or 10% TSP (Trisodium phosphate).

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced slow-release nutrition to minimize physiological plant stress.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: No chemical viricide exists; management focuses entirely on sanitation and vector exclusion.

organic_remedies.org1: Skim milk foliar spray (proteins inactivate and bind tobamovirus particles during transplanting).

disease_control.ctrl1: Carefully dig out and bag infected plants and root systems; discard in trash, do not compost.

disease_symptoms.s1: Dark brown to black angular spots with concentric target-like rings on older leaves.
disease_symptoms.s2: Chlorotic yellowing around leaf lesions leading to premature leaf senescence.
disease_symptoms.s3: Tubers develop sunken, dark, dry, corky rot with a purplish border beneath the skin.

disease_causes.c1: Warm weather (75°F - 85°F) with alternating wet periods and dry sunny days.
disease_causes.c2: Stressed plants (low nitrogen, drought, or heavy tuber bulking) are far more susceptible.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant certified disease-free seed tubers.
disease_prevention.p2: Maintain 3 to 4-year crop rotation away from solanaceous crops.
disease_prevention.p3: Irrigate in morning hours using drip methods; avoid overhead water.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced Potato Fertilizer (NPK 10-20-20 or 8-24-24) applied at planting and hilling.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Ensure adequate nitrogen early in the season to prevent premature vine senescence, but avoid late-season excess.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Supplement with Potassium and Magnesium to strengthen leaf cuticle.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Chlorothalonil (Bravo) or Mancozeb applied preventatively before row closure.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Azoxystrobin or Boscalid + Pyraclostrobin for targeted curative action.

organic_remedies.org1: Copper Hydroxide or Bordeaux mixture.

disease_control.ctrl1: Destroy infected potato vines 2 weeks prior to harvest to prevent tuber contamination during digging.
disease_control.ctrl2: Allow tuber skins to cure for 10-14 days at 55°F - 60°F before long-term storage.

disease_symptoms.s1: Irregular water-soaked black-brown lesions on leaves and stems.
disease_symptoms.s2: White cottony mildew growth on leaf undersides in wet morning dew.
disease_symptoms.s3: Entire potato canopy collapses and rots with an offensive odor.
disease_symptoms.s4: Tubers suffer brown granular dry rot extending several centimeters into the flesh.

disease_causes.c1: Cool, humid, rainy weather (60°F - 70°F) with high relative humidity (>90%).
disease_causes.c2: Infected seed tubers and cull potato piles left over winter.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant certified disease-free seed potatoes.
disease_prevention.p2: Hill soil well over developing tubers (at least 3-4 inches) to prevent zoospore wash-in from rain.
disease_prevention.p3: Destroy volunteer potatoes and cull piles completely.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: High-potash fertilizer (NPK 5-10-20) to enhance tuber skin set and storage life.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Avoid excess nitrogen fertilizer which extends tender vegetative susceptibility.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Cymoxanil, Mandipropamid, or Fluopicolide applied preventatively.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Mancozeb or Chlorothalonil before canopy closure.

organic_remedies.org1: Copper sulfate / Copper octanoate applied preventatively every 5 days during blight risk.

disease_control.ctrl1: Kill (flame or mow) potato vines immediately if late blight is detected; wait 2 weeks before harvesting tubers.
disease_control.ctrl2: Discard any soft or discolored tubers before storage.

disease_symptoms.s1: Lush, dark green, upright compound leaves with robust stems.
disease_symptoms.s2: White, pink, or purple flowers blossoming uniformly across rows.
disease_symptoms.s3: Clean subterranean stolons with smooth, firm, unblemished tubers.

disease_causes.c1: Cool weather, well-drained acidic soil (pH 5.5 - 6.5), and adequate moisture.

disease_prevention.p1: Hill plants with loose soil and straw as vines grow.
disease_prevention.p2: Inspect leaf undersides weekly for Colorado potato beetle egg clusters or early blight spots.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: NPK 10-15-15 fertilizer supplemented with Bone meal and greensand at hilling stage.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Maintain consistent soil moisture during tuber initiation and bulking.

organic_remedies.org1: Mulch deeply with straw to deter potato beetles and prevent tuber greening.

disease_control.ctrl1: Keep tubers well covered with soil to protect against greening and sun scald.

disease_symptoms.s1: Olive-green to dull brown velvety spots on upper and lower leaf surfaces.
disease_symptoms.s2: Mature lesions turn dark brown to black and develop a scabby, corky texture.
disease_symptoms.s3: Fruit develops scabby circular brown spots that crack open, stunting fruit growth.

disease_causes.c1: Overwinters in fallen infected leaves on orchard floor.
disease_causes.c2: Ascospores release during cool spring rains (55°F - 75°F / 13°C - 24°C) with prolonged leaf wetness (9+ hours).

disease_prevention.p1: Plant resistant cultivars (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Freedom, Pristine).
disease_prevention.p2: Rake and chop/compost or destroy fallen leaves in autumn to eradicate winter spore reserves.
disease_prevention.p3: Prune tree canopies annually to allow rapid wind drying of foliage.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced fruit tree fertilizer (NPK 10-10-10) applied early spring.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Apply Urea (5% foliar spray) in late autumn to speed leaf breakdown on the ground.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Captan or Mancozeb - Standard protective fungicides applied from green tip through petal fall.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Myclobutanil or Difenoconazole - Systemic curative post-infection fungicides.

organic_remedies.org1: Liquid Lime Sulfur or Wettable Sulfur applied early season.

disease_control.ctrl1: Begin fungicide sprays at green tip stage and repeat every 7-10 days until dry weather arrives.

disease_symptoms.s1: Small purple leaf spots that enlarge into circular lesions with light brown centers ('frog-eye' spots).
disease_symptoms.s2: Firm, brown rotting spots on fruit that develop dark concentric rings and turn coal-black (mummified).
disease_symptoms.s3: Sunken reddish-brown cankers on branches and limbs.

disease_causes.c1: Fungus survives in dead wood, mummified fruits, and bark cankers.
disease_causes.c2: Warm, wet weather (68°F - 75°F) with rain splash dispersing conidia.

disease_prevention.p1: Remove all mummified apples hanging on branches or on the ground during winter pruning.
disease_prevention.p2: Prune out dead wood, fire blight strikes, and cankers 6-8 inches below visible symptoms.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced organic orchard nutrition with compost and wood ash (Potassium).
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Avoid excessive nitrogen which promotes soft wood vulnerable to cankers.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Captan, Thiophanate-methyl, or Mancozeb applied from pink bud through harvest.

organic_remedies.org1: Copper Hydroxide dormant sprays in late winter.

disease_control.ctrl1: Prune out cankered limbs during dormant season and destroy wood immediately.

disease_symptoms.s1: Bright yellow-orange circular spots on upper surface of apple leaves.
disease_symptoms.s2: Underside of spots develops small cup-like tubes (aecia) that release orange spores in summer.
disease_symptoms.s3: Can cause leaf drop and raised orange bumpy spots on apple fruits near calyx end.

disease_causes.c1: Requires two hosts to complete life cycle: Apple/Crabapple and Eastern Red Cedar / Juniper.
disease_causes.c2: In spring, cedar galls produce gelatinous orange spore horns during rainy weather.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant resistant apple varieties (e.g., Liberty, Enterprise, Redfree, William's Pride).
disease_prevention.p2: Remove wild red cedars/junipers within several hundred feet of orchard if practical.
disease_prevention.p3: Prune and dispose of round brown cedar galls on nearby ornamental junipers.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Standard orchard NPK fertilizer with micronutrient zinc and boron.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Myclobutanil (Immunox) - Highly effective systemic fungicide for apple rust.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Mancozeb or Propiconazole applied from pink bud stage.

organic_remedies.org1: Sulfur-based fungicides applied before spring rain events.

disease_control.ctrl1: Apply protective fungicide when orange gelatinous horns appear on nearby cedars in spring.

disease_symptoms.s1: Dark green, crisp, unblemished foliage with clean veins.
disease_symptoms.s2: Strong terminal shoot extension and abundant healthy fruit spurs.
disease_symptoms.s3: Smooth bark, sound scaffolding branches, and unblemished growing fruits.

disease_causes.c1: Good orchard management, annual pruning, and balanced soil fertility.

disease_prevention.p1: Annual dormant winter pruning to open center canopy to sunlight.
disease_prevention.p2: Thin fruit clusters to 1 apple per cluster for maximum size and disease avoidance.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: NPK 12-12-12 or 10-10-10 applied in early spring around outer drip line.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Foliar Calcium Chloride sprays mid-summer to prevent bitter pit disorder in apples.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Dormant horticultural oil spray in late winter to smother overwintering scale and mite eggs.

organic_remedies.org1: Apply kaolin clay (Surround WP) to protect fruit from sunburn and insect pests.

disease_control.ctrl1: Maintain clean orchard floor free of tall weeds and fallen debris.

disease_symptoms.s1: Healthy green leaves, robust cane growth, and sweet unblemished berries.
disease_symptoms.s2: Leaf margins show clean cellular integrity.
disease_symptoms.s3: Vigorous shoot and root growth.

disease_causes.c1: Balanced environmental conditions.
disease_causes.c2: Optimum cultural management.

disease_prevention.p1: Provide adequate plant spacing to allow continuous air circulation.
disease_prevention.p2: Water at the soil level using drip irrigation; keep leaves dry.
disease_prevention.p3: Practice strict 3-year crop rotation and sanitize pruning equipment with 70% alcohol.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Apply balanced NPK formulation suitable for Blueberry (e.g. NPK 10-10-10 or 5-10-15).
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Supplement with Potassium and Calcium to reinforce plant cell walls against infection.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Avoid excessive nitrogen fertilizers that generate soft, vulnerable tissue.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: None needed.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Dormant copper sprays in winter to eliminate overwintering spores.

organic_remedies.org1: Cold-pressed Neem Oil spray (1% concentration) applied every 7 days.
organic_remedies.org2: Bio-fungicides based on Bacillus subtilis or Trichoderma viride.
organic_remedies.org3: Potassium Bicarbonate foliar wash (1 tbsp per gallon water) to suppress sporulation.

disease_control.ctrl1: Continue regular maintenance and weeding.
disease_control.ctrl2: Inspect crops weekly for early detection of pest and fungal hotspots.

disease_symptoms.s1: In tomato , Erwinia carotovora subsp
disease_symptoms.s2: carotovora or Pectobacterium carovora causes bacterial stem rot as well as soft rot

disease_causes.c1: Erwinia carotovora subsp

disease_causes.c3: It can survive as epiphytic bacteria on various plants or in the soil in low densities
disease_causes.c4: It has also been found in the gut of insects, possibly spreading from decaying vegetation to the growing crop that way

disease_symptoms.s1: Powdery mildew symptoms are fairly similar in all plant-pathogen combinations
disease_symptoms.s2: The symptoms are white fluffy colonies, first and foremost on the upper side of the leaf
disease_symptoms.s3: In severe epidemics in cereals, the ears may also be infected
disease_symptoms.s4: In pepper , the fluffy colonies occur mostly on the underside of the leaf, because the fungus infects the plant by entering through the stomata and there are more stomata on the underside of the leaf

disease_causes.c1: The fungi that cause powdery mildew ( Erysiphe, Podosphaera, Oïdium, Leveillula ) are all biotrophic fungi, meaning they feed on living plant cells and barely survive in the absence of a living crop
disease_causes.c2: They survive as ascospores or perithecia, structures containing ascospores
disease_causes.c3: Ascospores have not been found yet for all powdery mildew fungi and especially in greenhouse crops they don’t play a role in the epidemics
disease_causes.c4: Fungal spores germinate on the leaf surface and the germ tubes grow and branch out on the leaf surface

disease_prevention.p1: Use resistant cultivars whenever available Extra Silicon and/or Calcium nutrition hardens the cell walls and makes it harder for the fungi to enter the leaves To reduce chances of powdery mildew in greenhouses, it is advised to first ventilate by only opening the windows on the lee side
disease_prevention.p2: Please note, this is not relevant for other diseases that are inhibited by reducing the RH In fruit trees, pruning should be done early in the season Do not provide excess nitrogen since this promotes the disease Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.
disease_prevention.p3: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_symptoms.s1: Fusarium fungi cause vascular wilt, root rot, foot and stem rot, leaf lesions, fruit rot, head blight in cereals, and post-harvest decay
disease_symptoms.s2: Fusarium oxysporum (Fusarium wilt) is the species that causes vascular wilt
disease_symptoms.s3: Initially, the leaves turn yellow and wilt, mostly on one side of the plant
disease_symptoms.s4: Finally, the whole plant wilts

disease_causes.c1: Fusarium is a group of soil-borne fungi with many different species
disease_causes.c2: Fusarium is widespread and can infect a range of host crops
disease_causes.c3: Many species are considered weak pathogens, which can only infect wounded or stressed host plants
disease_causes.c4: Fusarium oxysporum has many different ‘formae speciales&rsquo

disease_symptoms.s1: In potato , field symptoms of Ralstonia solanacearum are wilting and yellowing of leaves and stunted plants
disease_symptoms.s2: Inside, vascular browning is common with bacterial slime oozing from the cut
disease_symptoms.s3: When the bacteria transfers to young plants through infected tubers, the wilting and collapse of plants happens rapidly
disease_symptoms.s4: Leaves remain green after wilting, until they are completely desiccated

disease_causes.c1: Ralstonia solanacearum is a quarantine organism in Europe and considered a bioterrorist organism in the United States
disease_causes.c2: It is a commonly found soil-inhabitant in tropical and subtropical regions and is transferred by the introduction of propagation materials (seed potatoes, cuttings of ornamentals ) from warmer regions
disease_causes.c3: Different races are distinguished with a differing, but overlapping host-range
disease_causes.c4: Race 3 is pretty much restricted to potato and tomato

disease_prevention.p1: Use disease free propagation materials (seed, cuttings, tubers) Disinfect cutting knives and tools Control root rot nematodes as the wounds they make on roots help the bacteria to infect the crop Do not use cut potatoes for propagation, since cutting tubers can increase disease incidence with up to 250% Quarantine measures are in place, including a five-year ban on using a field for potato cropping after infection of potatoes from that field has been established Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.

disease_causes.c1: Black rot of carrots ( Alternaria radicina ) is a seed-transferred carrot disease
disease_causes.c2: The seeds are the main source of primary infection and this may lead to death of seedlings

disease_causes.c4: Lesions of black rot of carrots ( Alternaria radicina ) may occasionally appear on the carrots at harvest but usually occur only during post-harvest storage

disease_prevention.p2: Use clean seed and propagation materials
disease_prevention.p3: Practice crop rotation, in particular when spores surviving in the soil are the main source of infection
disease_prevention.p4: Especially wheat and barley reduce the number of surviving conidia in the soil

disease_symptoms.s1: Pythium affects roots, in particular those of seedlings
disease_symptoms.s2: Infected plants lag in growth
disease_symptoms.s3: Seedlings start falling over, also called ‘damping-off’, hence the name damping-off disease
disease_symptoms.s4: In slightly older plants, the leaves lose their turgor or the leaf tips turn yellow, for example in flower bulbs

disease_causes.c1: Pythium belongs to the Oomycetes, a separate group of microorganisms and is therefore not a real fungus
disease_causes.c2: It survives as oospores, resting spores which are resistant to unfavourable conditions, especially dehydration
disease_causes.c3: Germination of the oospores is stimulated by exudates from roots of a susceptible host nearby
disease_causes.c4: The oospores germinate and form so-called sporangia from which subsequently zoospores are produced

disease_symptoms.s1: Pythium affects roots, in particular those of seedlings
disease_symptoms.s2: Infected plants lag in growth
disease_symptoms.s3: Seedlings fall over (&lsquo
disease_symptoms.s4: damping-off ’)

disease_causes.c1: Pythium belongs to the Oomycetes, a separate group of microorganisms and is therefore not a real fungus
disease_causes.c2: It survives as oospores, resting spores which are resistant to unfavourable conditions, especially dehydration
disease_causes.c3: Germination of the oospores is stimulated by exudates from roots of a susceptible host nearby
disease_causes.c4: The oospores germinate and form so-called sporangia from which subsequently zoospores are produced

disease_prevention.p1: Use resistant cultivars or graft on tolerant cultivars Use clean planting material Ensure regular growth Avoid over-watering Do not provide excess nitrogen since this promotes the disease
disease_prevention.p2: In greenhouses: Prevent high temperatures immediately after planting
disease_prevention.p3: Avoid cold and excessive warm irrigation water
disease_prevention.p4: Keep the water content of the substrate below 70% and ensure good drainage Disinfect recirculating nutrient solutions Increase the distance to the main substrate at the start by using higher substrate blocks for the seedlings In field crops: Avoid the use of fields with inadequate drainage or improve the drainage before planting/sowing Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.

disease_symptoms.s1: Phytophthora causes root rot, seedling damping off and rot of stems, bulbs, tubers, leaves and fruits
disease_symptoms.s2: Several Phytophthora species cause root- and crown rot in potted plants
disease_symptoms.s3: The small roots die and brown-black lesions occur on the larger roots
disease_symptoms.s4: Plants wilt and the crown leaves drop off.

disease_causes.c1: Phytophthora species are very destructive organisms belonging to the Oomycetes and are therefore strictly speaking not fungi
disease_causes.c2: They thrive at soil temperatures between 15 and 23 °C and higher water content than is optimal for crop growth
disease_causes.c3: Phytophthora overwinters in roots, infected tubers and bulbs or in the soil in different stages: as oospores (sexual overwintering spores), sporangia (special structures which can either germinate directly or produce zoospores), chlamydospores (thick-walled mycelium cells which are resistant to desiccation) or mycelium
disease_causes.c4: Zoospores are formed from the overwintering structures which infect the host

disease_prevention.p1: Apply hygiene measures, like cleaning machinery and tools, destroy waste heaps, remove remaining roots, infested leaves Choose less susceptible or resistant cultivars when available Prevent over-irrigating and be careful with overhead irrigation since both a high water content of the soil and water splash promote disease
disease_prevention.p2: Ensure fast drying and wound healing, by allowing air circulation Disinfect recirculating nutrient solutions Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.
disease_prevention.p3: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.
disease_prevention.p4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_causes.c4: The teliospores that are formed on systemically infected seeds then infect neighbouring new seeds

disease_symptoms.s1: Xanthomonas fragariae initially causes small, water-soaked lesions on the underside of the leaf
disease_symptoms.s2: They enlarge to angular spots, often limited by the small veins
disease_symptoms.s3: The distinctive feature is the way the lesions look when using different light sources: when reflected light is used, the lesions look dark green, but when transmitted light is used, they are translucent
disease_symptoms.s4: When conditions are humid, a viscous bacterial exudate forms on the underside of the leaf

disease_causes.c1: Xanthomonas fragariae overwinters in plants and dead leaves, that become the primary source of infection in the spring
disease_causes.c2: The bacteria are also introduced in a crop in new transplants
disease_causes.c3: This bacterium is very resistant to desiccation and can survive well in dry leaves or leaves in the soil, but not independantly in the soil
disease_causes.c4: Under humid conditions, bacteria ooze from the lesions on the leaves and form a secondary source of infection

disease_symptoms.s1: Phomopsis sclerotioides causes grey-black spots with a dark demarcation line on cucumber roots
disease_symptoms.s2: The lesions are slightly sunken and are mostly formed around the point of attachment of lateral roots and root hairs
disease_symptoms.s3: The lesions may grow and encircle the root
disease_symptoms.s4: The roots become yellow-brown to black and ultimately die

disease_causes.c1: Phomopsis sclerotioides survives in the soil and is a strong saprophytic competitor, which means it can rapidly colonize ‘clean’ or sterilized soil and substrate
disease_causes.c2: It aggregates, so disinfection needs to be applied thoroughly and evenly
disease_causes.c3: Phomopsis sclerotioides forms sclerotia which can survive adverse conditions for years in the soil, but little else is known about the life cycle
disease_causes.c4: The fungus is dispersed by water, air and soil particles.

disease_prevention.p1: Test for the presence of Phomopsis sclerotioides with molecular tools before planting Use resistant rootstock of Cucurbita ficifolia Apply steam sterilization to the soil/substrate Fumigation with soil disinfectants is only effective when applied evenly Note: since this fungus can rapidly re-colonize the soil/substrate, disinfection should be applied at least annually Disinfect nutrient solution and irrigation water Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.

disease_symptoms.s1: Phomopsis sclerotioides causes grey-black spots with a dark demarcation line on cucumber roots

disease_causes.c3: Phomopsis sclerotioides forms sclerotia which can survive adverse conditions for years in the soil, but little else is known about the life cycle
disease_causes.c4: The fungus is dispersed by water, air and soil particles.

disease_symptoms.s1: The first signs of this disease, are poorly looking plants in localized areas of the greenhouse or field
disease_symptoms.s2: The affected plants may wilt
disease_symptoms.s3: Also, interveinal chlorosis of leaves and premature defoliation may occur
disease_symptoms.s4: Looking at the roots, there are three different symptoms

disease_causes.c1: Pyrenochaeta lycopersici survives in the soil and in buried tomato roots as microsclerotia

disease_causes.c3: Several alternate hosts in outdoor cropping systems are known: pepper , melon , aubergine, squash, spinach and safflower
disease_causes.c4: The disease develops between 8 and 32 °C, but the fungus prefers low temperatures

disease_symptoms.s1: Phytophthora cactorum causes seedling damping off, a reduced root system and black discolouration of the roots
disease_symptoms.s2: On the foot, dark brown lesions with sharp borders occur
disease_symptoms.s3: Above the graft and on leaves, dark brown, irregular lesions occur
disease_symptoms.s4: In strawberry , the heart leaves wilt first, then the whole plant.

disease_causes.c1: Phytophthora species are very destructive organisms belonging to the Oomycetes and are therefore strictly speaking not fungi
disease_causes.c2: They thrive at soil temperatures between 15 and 23 °C and higher water content than is optimal for crop growth
disease_causes.c3: Phytophthora overwinters in roots, infected tubers and bulbs or in the soil in different stages: as oospores (sexual overwintering spores), sporangia (special structures which can either germinate directly or produce zoospores), chlamydospores (thick-walled mycelium cells which are resistant to desiccation) or mycelium
disease_causes.c4: Zoospores are formed from the overwintering structures, which infect the host

disease_prevention.p1: Apply hygiene measures, like cleaning machinery and tools, destroy waste heaps, remove remaining roots, infested leaves Choose less susceptible or resistant cultivars when available Prevent over-irrigating and be careful with overhead irrigation since both a high water content of the soil and water splash promote disease
disease_prevention.p2: Ensure fast drying and wound healing, by allowing air circulation Disinfect recirculating nutrient solutions Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.

disease_symptoms.s1: The four pathogenic Rhizobium species cause different symptoms, like galls, tumours and excessive root growth
disease_symptoms.s2: All four species cause the growth of galls on the stems, which are first white and later turn brown
disease_symptoms.s3: Only Rhizobium radiobacter causes galls and tumours on underground plant parts and on the crown
disease_symptoms.s4: Furthermore, infection is characterized by excessive root growth (crazy roots)

disease_causes.c1: The primary source of infection by Rhizobium rhizogenes has not yet been defined
disease_causes.c2: The assumption is that the bacteria survive in the soil, but it is possible that first infection is from the propagation material
disease_causes.c3: Infection also takes place via wounds
disease_causes.c4: After infection, galls are formed which break open, releasing many bacteria

disease_symptoms.s1: The four pathogenic Rhizobium species cause different symptoms, like galls, tumours and excessive root growth
disease_symptoms.s2: All four species cause the growth of galls on the stems, which are first white and later turn brown
disease_symptoms.s3: Only Rhizobium radiobacter causes galls and tumours on underground plant parts and on the crown
disease_symptoms.s4: Furthermore, infection is characterized by excessive root growth (crazy roots)

disease_causes.c1: The primary source of infection by Rhizobium rhizogenes has not yet been defined
disease_causes.c2: The assumption is that the bacteria survive in the soil, but it is possible that first infection is from the propagation material
disease_causes.c3: Infection also takes place via wounds
disease_causes.c4: After infection, galls are formed which break open, releasing many bacteria

disease_prevention.p2: Adjust the work order in greenhouses to fit with the hygiene protocol Disinfect the nutrient solution in order to prevent biofilm growth inside the irrigation system Prevent contact between the plant roots and the gutters in greenhouses Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.

disease_symptoms.s1: Downy mildew pathogens infect mostly the leaves but occasionally also stems and fruits

disease_symptoms.s3: On the underside of the leave fluffy growth appears which is first white and later turns grey-brown
disease_symptoms.s4: This is actually the sporulation of the pathogens extruding from the stomata.

disease_causes.c1: Pathogens causing downy mildew are not fungi but Oomycetes and related to Pythium and Phytophthora
disease_causes.c2: They survive as oospores
disease_causes.c3: From these oospores or surviving mycelium sporangia are formed, structures in which zoospores are produced
disease_causes.c4: However, in downy mildews, sporangia often germinate directly and the germ tubes infect the plants either through the stomata or directly by penetrating the cuticula

disease_prevention.p1: Choose resistant cultivars Use a wide crop rotation with non-host crops Prevent a humid microclimate
disease_prevention.p2: Achieve this by lowering crop density, good aeration during propagation and maintaining a warm and dry climate in greenhouses
disease_prevention.p3: Use hygiene measures
disease_prevention.p4: Start clean, remove crop residues and prevent splashing water

disease_symptoms.s1: Alternaria solani causes small green to dark brown spots to occur on leaves
disease_symptoms.s2: Those spots then turn into dark brown angular lesions with a yellow halo restricted by leaf veins
disease_symptoms.s3: Lesions can easily rupture
disease_symptoms.s4: Other symptoms are brown lesions on stem and foot

disease_causes.c1: From the primary infection of leaves, Alternaria solani can spread to the flowers (especially dangerous in crops for seed production) and to the crown
disease_causes.c2: Sporulation of Alternaria occurs at temperatures from 2-4 °C up to 28-30 °C (optimum temperatures lie between 15 and 28 °C) and at a relative humidity (RH) of over 90% or when the leaves are wet
disease_causes.c3: Small differences in optimum temperature occur between species, but in general the risk of Alternaria infection is larger under quite warm and humid conditions
disease_causes.c4: Infection may take place within a few hours, with lesions occurring as rapidly as two to three days later and sporulation within five days

disease_prevention.p1: Remove crop residues, weeds and volunteer plants
disease_prevention.p2: Use clean seed and propagation materials
disease_prevention.p3: Practice crop rotation, in particular when spores surviving in the soil are the main source of infection
disease_prevention.p4: Especially wheat and barley reduce the number of surviving conidia in the soil

disease_symptoms.s1: Fusarium fungi cause vascular wilt, root rot, foot and stem rot, leaf lesions, fruit rot, head blight in cereals and post-harvest decay
disease_symptoms.s2: Fusarium oxysporum is the species causing vascular wilt
disease_symptoms.s3: First the leaves turn yellow and wilt, mostly on one side of the plant
disease_symptoms.s4: Finally, the whole plant wilts

disease_causes.c1: Fusarium oxysporum has many different formae speciales which are each selectively pathogenic on a limited number of crops
disease_causes.c2: Even within one crop, different formae speciales may occur and cause different symptoms
disease_causes.c3: Fusarium oxysporum is the only Fusarium that actually grows inside the vessel system of the host plant and spreads upwards inside the plants
disease_causes.c4: The other species are dispersed upwards on the outside of the plant

disease_symptoms.s1: Mycosphaerella cucumis in cucumber causes brown lesions on the foot and higher up on the stem
disease_symptoms.s2: On the lesions, golden-brown gummy drops occur, hence the name gummy stem blight
disease_symptoms.s3: On the lesions, black specks, the new fruiting bodies with spores, become visible
disease_symptoms.s4: On the leaves, round and extending lesions may occur

disease_causes.c1: Mycosphaerella cucumis survives in crop debris and produces the sexual ascospores and asexual conida simultaneously
disease_causes.c2: The spores germinate when free water is present on the plant, at high relative humidity (RH) and on wounds
disease_causes.c3: Leaves can be infected directly, through wounds, hydathodes (the end of leaf veins) or the hair bases
disease_causes.c4: Stems are infected through wounds and by the infected leaves through the petioles

disease_symptoms.s1: Mycosphaerella cucumis in cucumber causes brown lesions on the foot and higher up on the stem
disease_symptoms.s2: On the lesions, golden-brown gummy drops occur, hence the name gummy stem blight
disease_symptoms.s3: On the lesions, black specks, the new fruiting bodies with spores, become visible
disease_symptoms.s4: On the leaves, round and extending lesions may occur

disease_causes.c1: Mycosphaerella cucumis survives in crop debris and produces the sexual ascospores and asexual conida simultaneously
disease_causes.c2: The spores germinate when free water is present on the plant, at high relative humidity (RH) and on wounds
disease_causes.c3: Leaves can be infected directly, through wounds, hydathodes (the end of leaf veins) or the hair bases
disease_causes.c4: Stems are infected through wounds and by the infected leaves through the petioles

disease_prevention.p1: Before cropping: Remove all crop debris and disinfect the greenhouse Choose a cultivar that is less susceptible to internal fruit rot Use clean propagation material During cropping and between consecutive cucumber crops: Remove all pots and plant parts from previous crop that may serve as inoculum source for the new crop prevent condensation on all plant parts at all times Extra Silicon and/or Calcium nutrition hardens the cell walls and makes it harder for the fungi to enter the leaves Pick flowers within two days after opening in areas suspected of disease (only feasible in high-wire crops) Pick and remove dead and diseased leaves Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.

disease_symptoms.s1: Symptoms of grape downy mildew (Plasmopara viticola) vary according to the crop’s growth stage, environmental conditions, and infection pressure
disease_symptoms.s2: While all green tissues of the grapevine are susceptible, characteristic ‘oil spots&rsquo
disease_symptoms.s3: on the upper surface of young, actively growing leaves, followed by downy white growth on the underside, are typical early symptoms
disease_symptoms.s4: Because visible symptoms usually appear 7–10 days post-infection (depending on temperature and humidity), the disease is often well-established before it can be visually detected in the field.

disease_causes.c1: Plasmopara viticola is an obligate biotrophic pathogen of grapevines, characterized by sexual overwintering and rapid asexual cycles during the growing season
disease_causes.c2: The pathogen overwinters primarily as oospores in fallen leaf litter, though in milder climates it can also persist as mycelium within infected buds and canes
disease_causes.c3: In spring, oospore germination is triggered when temperatures reach 10°C in the presence of soil moisture, leading to the formation of macrosporangia that release motile zoospores within 24 hours
disease_causes.c4: These zoospores are dispersed via rain splash to the canopy, where they encyst and penetrate the host through stomata

disease_prevention.p1: Effective management of grape downy mildew (Plasmopara viticola) relies on a preventive and integrated approach
disease_prevention.p2: Since the pathogen remains latent before symptoms emerge, control strategies should focus on reducing infection pressure, limiting favorable conditions for disease development, and maintaining protective coverage on susceptible tissues during high-risk periods.
disease_prevention.p3: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.
disease_prevention.p4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_symptoms.s1: In strawberry , this pathogen causes wilting of foliage, stunting of plants and drying and death of older leaves
disease_symptoms.s2: The youngest central leaves usually remain unaffected and stay green
disease_symptoms.s3: The first symptoms are mostly found after plants are well established and after plants begin bearing fruit or are subjected to stress
disease_symptoms.s4: Severely infected plants collapse and die

disease_causes.c1: The fungus survives in the soil and on crop residues as microsclerotia
disease_causes.c2: In corn stalks, survival of up to 1.5 years has been reported
disease_causes.c3: The density of the microsclerotia in the soil is directly related to disease incidence
disease_causes.c4: Within 24 hours the fungus infects the roots of the host by direct penetration via germ tubes

disease_symptoms.s2: Late blight or Phytophthora blight (Phytophtora infestans f.sp
disease_symptoms.s3: infestans ) causes water-soaked lesions with vague borders and white fluffy fungal growth on the leaves
disease_symptoms.s4: The centre is grey-brown with a light-green edge

disease_causes.c1: Phytophthora species are very destructive organisms belonging to the Oomycetes and are therefore strictly speaking not fungi
disease_causes.c2: They thrive at soil temperatures between 15 and 23 °C and higher water content than is optimal for crop growth
disease_causes.c3: Phytophthora overwinters in roots, infected tubers and bulbs or in the soil in different stages: as oospores (sexual overwintering spores), sporangia (special structures which can either germinate directly or produce zoospores), chlamydospores (thick-walled mycelium cells which are resistant to desiccation) or mycelium
disease_causes.c4: Zoospores are formed from the overwintering structures which infect the host

disease_symptoms.s1: Fusarium fungi cause vascular wilt, root rot, foot and stem rot, leaf lesions, fruit rot, fusarium head blight in cereals, such as wheat (fusarium head blight wheat) and post-harvest decay.
disease_symptoms.s2: Stunted vegetative growth and reduced photosynthetic vigor.
disease_symptoms.s3: Premature leaf chlorosis, yellowing, and leaf drop.
disease_symptoms.s4: Blemishes, corky scars, or rots on harvested plant organs and fruit.

disease_causes.c1: Most Fusarium species only make asexual spores
disease_causes.c2: Some also produce ascospores
disease_causes.c3: In general, most Fusarium specieshave a similar life cycle
disease_causes.c4: Fusarium overwinters for many years in the soil and on crop residues of infected plants as chlamydospores (thick walled mycelium cells) or mycelium

disease_symptoms.s1: Tilletia controversa causes (bunted) heads that are slender and remain green longer than healthy heads
disease_symptoms.s2: The glumes are opened either on some or on all spikelets, showing the bunt (smut spore) they contain, which is larger than a normal kernel
disease_symptoms.s3: The bunt balls are grey-brown
disease_symptoms.s4: They rupture at harvest and release black, powdery spores, that smell like fish, hence the common name stinking bunt

disease_causes.c1: Tilletia controversa survives as teliospores in the soil or on seed
disease_causes.c2: The soil-borne teliospores are the main source of primary infection
disease_causes.c3: The soil-borne teliospores may survive in soil without suitable host for as long as ten years
disease_causes.c4: Seed-borne transmission does occur, but is less important from an epidemiological point of view

disease_prevention.p1: Use resistant cultivars
disease_prevention.p2: However, the fungi may form new isolates that can break resistance Use clean, disinfected seed The use of soil fungicides can help reduce the soil-borne inoculum Sowing winter crops early in the fall when temperatures are still above 15°C at the critical first 11 days reduces the risk of infection by Triticum tritici and Triticum laevis
disease_prevention.p3: Since Triticum controversa mostly attacks the 2-3 leaf stage, this is less effective for this fungus Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.
disease_prevention.p4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_symptoms.s1: Ascochyta pisi causes spots on leaves, stems and pods of peas
disease_symptoms.s2: The spots on leaves and pods are round, on the stems they are more elongated
disease_symptoms.s3: The lesions are light brown, sunken and surrounded by a dark brown to red-brown border
disease_symptoms.s4: The first infection is often on the primary leaves

disease_causes.c1: Ascochyta pisi hardly survives in the soil or on crop residues because of its poor saprophytic competitiveness and because chlamydospores are rare
disease_causes.c2: Primary infection is purely seed-borne
disease_causes.c3: Conidia and other fungal structures are transmitted on the outside of the seed coat and cause primary infection
disease_causes.c4: The conidia germinate and infect through the stomata or directly through the cuticle

Horticultural___agricultural_crops___Roo.disease_name: Root and crown rot of strawberry

disease_symptoms.s1: Pestalotiopsis clavispora causes discoloration or brown necrotic areas in crown and root of strawberry
disease_symptoms.s2: Plant development is slow, growth is retarded and rooting is poor
disease_symptoms.s3: Transplants look weak and may die
disease_symptoms.s4: It is hard to visually distinguish between Pestalotiopsis clavispora and Phytophthora cactorum .

disease_causes.c1: Not much is known about the life cycle
disease_causes.c2: The fungus produces ascospores and conidia, but their role in the epidemic has not yet been established
disease_causes.c3: Pestalotiopsis clavispora is mostly found in plants that have been weakened by some form of stress, from underfertilization to water stress (either too much or too little water), or that are damaged by for example handling or pests
disease_causes.c4: Optimum temperature for Pestalotiopsis clavispora is 19-23 °C and high humidity or free water stimulates disease development.

disease_symptoms.s1: Rhexocercosporidium carotae is a slow-growing fungus that can infect both roots and foliage
disease_symptoms.s2: The infection starts with small black spots over the entire surface of the carrot
disease_symptoms.s3: These spots gradually change into larger dark brown to black lesions of various shapes
disease_symptoms.s4: The lesions can merge and eventually cover the entire surface of the carrot

disease_causes.c1: carotae has delicate, simple morphological features hence is not easy to place it at the generic level
disease_causes.c2: Årsvoll was the first to identify and describe the fungus in Norway, in 1965
disease_causes.c3: An infection can occur through the soil and the air
disease_causes.c4: The fungus develops at temperatures ranging from -3°C to 25°C, with an optimum around 18°C

disease_prevention.p1: Studies have shown that 3several key factors influencing the occurrence of blemishes and the presence of Rhexocercosporidium carotae in carrot roots: Mechanical damages: Pathogenic fungi often enter through wounds formed during harvest
disease_prevention.p2: Pre-storage treatments to harden the periderm and heal wounds may help control infections, but preventing contamination is more effective
disease_prevention.p3: Topping efficiency: Mechanical harvesting always causes some damage to carrot roots, which can be infected by Rhexocercosporidium carotae
disease_prevention.p4: Pre-storage treatments to harden the periderm and heal wounds may help control infections

disease_causes.c1: Verticillium dahliae survives for prolonged time periods (many years) in the soil as microsclerotia, small hard survival structures that can withstand high and low temperatures and dehydration
disease_causes.c2: Verticillium dahliae also survives as hyphae (mycelium) in crop residues
disease_causes.c3: The fungus infects the roots of plants, directly or through wounds caused by for example nematodes
disease_causes.c4: The fungus then grows into the vessels of the plant and produces spores that are transported upwards with the transpiration stream

disease_symptoms.s1: Plantsinfected by Tilletia tritici and Tilletia laevis are hard to distinguish from infected plants before head emergence, although affected plants may be slightly stunted
disease_symptoms.s2: Infected (bunted) heads are slender and remain green longer than healthy heads
disease_symptoms.s3: The glumes are opened either on some or on all spikelets, showing the bunt (smut spore) they contain, which is larger than a normal kernel
disease_symptoms.s4: The bunt balls are grey-brown

disease_causes.c1: Tilletia tritici and Tilletia laevis survive as teliospores in the soil or on seed
disease_causes.c2: These teliospores germinate in response to moisture and form basidiospores, also called primary sporidium
disease_causes.c3: Two mating types are distinguished
disease_causes.c4: The filiform basidiospores fuse in the middle with a basidiospore of the other mating type so that H-shaped structures are formed

disease_prevention.p3: Since Triticum controversa mostly attacks the 2-3 leaf stage, this is less effective for this fungus Prevent plant diseases by optimizing plant potential and crop resilience.

disease_symptoms.s3: Kresek phase causes entire young seedling wilting and death.
disease_symptoms.s4: Blemishes, corky scars, or rots on harvested plant organs and fruit.

disease_causes.c1: Survives in seed hulls, stubble, and irrigation canals
disease_causes.c2: Enters leaves via hydathodes at leaf margins and mechanical wounds created by typhoon winds or farm tools.
disease_causes.c3: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.
disease_causes.c4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant resistant cultivars carrying Xa-gene resistance (e.g., Xa21)
disease_prevention.p2: Ensure balanced N-P-K fertilization (excess nitrogen increases severity)
disease_prevention.p3: Drain excess water from fields.
disease_prevention.p4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced N-P-K plant nutrition tailored to crop stage; avoid excessive nitrogen.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Apply Potassium (K) (Sulfate of Potash) to reinforce plant vascular tissue and cell wall rigidity.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Supplement with soluble Calcium (Calcium Nitrate) and Silicon to thicken leaf epidermal barriers.
fertilizer_recommendation.f4: Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost to enrich beneficial soil microbial antagonists.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf1: Seed soaking in streptocycline (100 ppm) + copper oxychloride solution. Foliar spraying with copper hydroxide or validamycin. Bio-inoculants with Pseudomonas fluorescens seed treatment.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Mancozeb (0.2%) or Chlorothalonil contact protectant before anticipated wet weather.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Azoxystrobin or Difenoconazole systemic treatment where permitted.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf4: Soil drench with bio-inoculant Trichoderma harzianum or Streptomyces lydicus.

organic_remedies.org1: Seed soaking in streptocycline (100 ppm) + copper oxychloride solution. Foliar spraying with copper hydroxide or validamycin. Bio-inoculants with Pseudomonas fluorescens seed treatment.
organic_remedies.org2: Koppert Veni GoKlean / Bacillus subtilis bio-protection foliar spray.
organic_remedies.org3: Cold-pressed Neem Seed Kernel Extract (NSKE 5%) or horticultural botanical oil.
organic_remedies.org4: Potassium bicarbonate spray (5 g/L) to alter leaf surface pH and suppress pathogens.

disease_control.dc1: Prune out and immediately incinerate or bury visibly infected tissues.
disease_control.dc2: Sterilize all pruning shears, knives, and equipment with 70% isopropyl alcohol.
disease_control.dc3: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; irrigate strictly at the root zone via drip lines.
disease_control.dc4: Apply targeted bio-fungicide or bactericide at earliest detection of initial symptoms.

disease_symptoms.s1: Rough, abnormal, tumor-like swellings (galls) on roots, crown (ground level), and woody lower stems
disease_symptoms.s2: Young galls are spongy and flesh-colored
disease_symptoms.s3: older galls turn hard, woody, dark brown, and fissured.
disease_symptoms.s4: Blemishes, corky scars, or rots on harvested plant organs and fruit.

disease_causes.c1: Bacterium enters root or stem wounds caused by grafting, cultivation, root insects, or pruning
disease_causes.c2: It transfers a segment of its Ti-plasmid (T-DNA) into host plant cells, directing host cells to overproduce auxins and cytokinins (causing hyperplasia and hypertrophy).
disease_causes.c3: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.
disease_causes.c4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_prevention.p1: Plant certified disease-free nursery stock
disease_prevention.p2: Avoid wounding stems and crowns during planting and weed cultivation
disease_prevention.p3: Sanitize budding knives with alcohol.
disease_prevention.p4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_causes.c3: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.
disease_causes.c4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_symptoms.s4: Blemishes, corky scars, or rots on harvested plant organs and fruit.

Mango___Anthracnose.scientific_name: Colletotrichum gloeosporioides / Colletotrichum acutatum / Colletotrichum lindemuthianum

disease_symptoms.s1: Dark brown to black sunken circular necrotic lesions on foliage, stems, flowers, and fruit
disease_symptoms.s2: Under moist humid conditions, concentric salmon-pink or orange gelatinous spore masses (acervuli) erupt in lesion centers.
disease_symptoms.s3: Premature leaf chlorosis, yellowing, and leaf drop.
disease_symptoms.s4: Blemishes, corky scars, or rots on harvested plant organs and fruit.

disease_causes.c1: Survives as dormant mycelium or appressoria on plant debris, seed coats, or infected twigs
disease_causes.c2: Conidia are spread by splashing raindrops and wind-driven mist
disease_causes.c3: Fungi penetrate cuticle directly via specialized melanized appressoria.
disease_causes.c4: Maintain field sanitation and crop health.

disease_prevention.p1: Use certified disease-free seeds
disease_prevention.p2: Prune dense canopies to promote rapid drying of foliage
disease_prevention.p3: Remove fallen leaves and mummified fruits
disease_prevention.p4: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation.

fertilizer_recommendation.f1: Balanced N-P-K plant nutrition tailored to crop stage; avoid excessive nitrogen.
fertilizer_recommendation.f2: Apply Potassium (K) (Sulfate of Potash) to reinforce plant vascular tissue and cell wall rigidity.
fertilizer_recommendation.f3: Supplement with soluble Calcium (Calcium Nitrate) and Silicon to thicken leaf epidermal barriers.
fertilizer_recommendation.f4: Incorporate well-decomposed organic compost to enrich beneficial soil microbial antagonists.

pesticides_and_fungicides.pf2: Mancozeb (0.2%) or Chlorothalonil contact protectant before anticipated wet weather.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf3: Azoxystrobin or Difenoconazole systemic treatment where permitted.
pesticides_and_fungicides.pf4: Soil drench with bio-inoculant Trichoderma harzianum or Streptomyces lydicus.

organic_remedies.org1: Biofungicides: Trichoderma harzianum (Trianum-P)
organic_remedies.org2: Bacillus subtilis (Veni GoKlean). Chemical fungicides: Azoxystrobin
organic_remedies.org4: Potassium bicarbonate spray (5 g/L) to alter leaf surface pH and suppress pathogens.

disease_control.dc1: Prune out and immediately incinerate or bury visibly infected tissues.
disease_control.dc2: Sterilize all pruning shears, knives, and equipment with 70% isopropyl alcohol.
disease_control.dc3: Avoid overhead sprinkler irrigation; irrigate strictly at the root zone via drip lines.
disease_control.dc4: Apply targeted bio-fungicide or bactericide at earliest detection of initial symptoms.
